claim: A potent class of HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) targets the envelope glycoprotein's membrane proximal exposed region (MPER).
source: A potent class of HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) targets the envelope glycoprotein's membrane proximal exposed region (MPER) through a proposed mechanism where hypervariable loops embed into lipid bilayers and engage headgroup moieties alongside the epitope.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the HIV research field, supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: MPER-targeting bnAbs use a mechanism where hypervariable loops embed into lipid bilayers and engage headgroup moieties alongside the epitope.
source: A potent class of HIV-1 broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) targets the envelope glycoprotein's membrane proximal exposed region (MPER) through a proposed mechanism where hypervariable loops embed into lipid bilayers and engage headgroup moieties alongside the epitope.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by previous experimental work cited in the manuscript.

claim: All-atom simulations of 4E10, PGZL1, 10E8, and LN01 docked onto HIV-like membranes consistently form phospholipid complexes at key complementarity-determining region loop sites.
source: All-atom simulations of 4E10, PGZL1, 10E8, and LN01 docked onto HIV-like membranes consistently form phospholipid complexes at key complementarity-determining region loop sites, solidifying that stable and specific lipid interactions anchor bnAbs to membrane surfaces.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the all-atom MD simulations performed in this study, supported by data shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Stable and specific lipid interactions anchor bnAbs to membrane surfaces.
source: All-atom simulations of 4E10, PGZL1, 10E8, and LN01 docked onto HIV-like membranes consistently form phospholipid complexes at key complementarity-determining region loop sites, solidifying that stable and specific lipid interactions anchor bnAbs to membrane surfaces.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the simulation data showing consistent phospholipid binding at specific CDR sites.

claim: Antibody framework regions make surprising contributions to protein-lipid contacts.
source: Ancillary protein-lipid contacts reveal surprising contributions from antibody framework regions.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the simulations, particularly the observation of FR-H3 interactions with membranes.

claim: Coarse-grained simulations effectively capture antibodies embedding into membranes.
source: Coarse-grained simulations effectively capture antibodies embedding into membranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CG simulation results shown in Figures 4-5.

claim: Bilayer affinity is evolved along the PGZL1 maturation pathway and correlates with neutralization potency.
source: Simulations estimating protein-membrane interaction strength for PGZL1 variants along an inferred maturation pathway show bilayer affinity is evolved and correlates with neutralization potency.
evidence: This is shown by the pulling simulation data in Figure 7 comparing germline, intermediate, and mature PGZL1 variants.

claim: B-cells producing antibodies targeting host membranes are downregulated in healthy organisms.
source: B-cells producing antibodies targeting host membranes are downregulated in healthy organisms (Goodnow et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2015; Verkoczy et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Rare antibodies with lipid affinity can emerge in cases of chronic inflammation and infection as in HIV.
source: Nonetheless, rare antibodies with lipid affinity can emerge, particularly in cases of chronic inflammation and infection as in HIV (Matyas et al., 2009; Alam et al., 2007; Alam et al., 2009; Haynes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: MPER-targeting bnAbs 4E10, PGZL1, 10E8, and LN01 stem from unique lineages.
source: We sought to address this phenomenon for broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) 4E10, PGZL1, 10E8, and LN01 which stem from unique lineages and all target the semi-concealed membrane-proximal epitope region (MPER) (Lee et al., 2016; Cardoso et al., 2007; Cardoso et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2008) of the HIV-1 envelope glycoprotein (Env).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MPER-targeting bnAbs show varying degrees of affinity for lipid components.
source: Interestingly, these bnAbs show varying degrees of affinity for lipid components; some associate with lipid bilayers or cultured cells even in the absence of antigen (Matyas et al., 2009; Alam et al., 2007; Alam et al., 2009; Haynes et al., 2005, Stiegler et al., 2001; Huang et al., 2012; Pinto et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Scherer et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental studies cited.

claim: Membrane interaction behavior of MPER bnAbs correlates with neutralization potency.
source: This membrane interaction behavior appears to correlate with neutralization potency and is attributed to shared CDR loop features including a long hydrophobic CDR-H3 (Alam et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2012; Scherer et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2014; Irimia et al., 2017; Kwon et al., 2018a; Zwick et al., 2004).
evidence: This correlation is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Mutations enhancing association to phospholipid vesicles boost efficacy of pseudovirus neutralization.
source: The correlation between membrane association and neutralization has been established, given that mutations or chemical conjugations to solvent-exposed antibody loop residues which enhance association to phospholipid vesicles consequently boost efficacy of pseudovirus neutralization (Rujas et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the cited study.

claim: Mutations reducing hydrophobicity in 4E10 CDR-H3 drastically reduce neutralization activity while weakening lipid bilayer association.
source: Conversely, mutations reducing hydrophobicity drastically reduce neutralization activity while also weakening association to lipid bilayers, despite minimal impacts to antigen affinity (e.g. 4E10 CDR-H3 H100-H102 Trp-Trp motif; PGZL1 clone H4K3's CDR-H1; Alam et al., 2009; Scherer et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2010; Julien et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multiple cited studies.

claim: Phospholipid membrane interactions evolved by MPER-targeting bnAbs are critical for their mechanism of immune protection against HIV.
source: Thus, phospholipid membrane interactions evolved by MPER-targeting bnAbs appear critical for their mechanism of immune protection against HIV.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental evidence showing correlation between membrane binding and neutralization.

claim: Cryo-EM of Env trimers bound to bnAbs PGZL1, 4E10, and 10E8 within model membranes suggest their CDR loops form intimate contacts with surrounding lipids while engaging MPER.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) of Env trimers bound to bnAbs PGZL1, 4E10, and 10E8 within in different model membranes suggest their CDR loops form intimate contacts with surrounding lipids while engaging MPER (Rantalainen et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structural data from cited studies.

claim: Fab crystal structures of MPER bnAbs soaked with short-chain phospholipids revealed ordered headgroup moieties complexed within the CDR loops.
source: Antigen binding fragments (Fab) crystal structures of those bnAbs as well as LN01 soaked with short-chain phospholipids all revealed ordered headgroup moieties complexed within the CDR loops in the presence and absence of antigen (Matyas et al., 2009; Haynes et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2016; Irimia et al., 2016) suggesting the antibodies encode specific lipid interactions (Matyas et al., 2009; Haynes et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2016; Irimia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallography data from multiple cited studies.

claim: A two-step bnAb neutralization mechanism is proposed wherein bnAbs first associate with membranes via embedding their CDRs, then laterally diffuse to engage Env at MPER.
source: These data support a two-step bnAb neutralization mechanism proposed previously, wherein a population of bnAbs in vivo may first associate with membranes via embedding their CDRs, then laterally diffuse across the bilayer surface to subsequently engage Env at MPER (Alam et al., 2007; Pinto et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2014; Irimia et al., 2017; Kwon et al., 2018a; Rantalainen et al., 2020; Irimia et al., 2016; Carravilla et al., 2020a; Soto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Unbiased all-atom MD simulations accurately and reproducibly predict ab initio binding of phospholipids at specific CDR binding sites previously identified in co-crystal structures.
source: We find that unbiased all-atom MD simulations accurately and reproducibly predict ab initio binding of phospholipids stably bound at specific CDR binding sites previously identified in co-crystal structures (Pinto et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2017; Irimia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MD simulations, validated against experimental structures.

claim: Four 1 μs pseudo-replicate simulations were initiated per bnAb for 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8.
source: Four 1 μs pseudo-replicate simulations were initiated per bnAb, with two replicates tilted by ± 15 degrees to modestly vary the starting membrane-interacting pose, utilizing an explicit simplified HIV-like model anionic bilayer: 25% cholesterol, 5% 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate (POPA), 70% 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC; Alam et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology used in the study.

claim: The HIV-like model membrane used in simulations contained 25% cholesterol, 5% POPA, and 70% POPC.
source: Four 1 μs pseudo-replicate simulations were initiated per bnAb, with two replicates tilted by ± 15 degrees to modestly vary the starting membrane-interacting pose, utilizing an explicit simplified HIV-like model anionic bilayer: 25% cholesterol, 5% 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphate (POPA), 70% 1-palmitoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (POPC; Alam et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the membrane composition used in simulations, based on a cited reference.

claim: 4E10 and PGZL1 are homologous with 85% sequence identity.
source: 4E10 and PGZL1 are homologous (85% sequence identity, sharing IgG VH1-69, VH4-34, and VH4-59), and have very similar affinities, breadths, and potencies (paricularly comparing 4E10 and PGZL1.H4K3).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the sequence similarity of these antibodies.

claim: 4E10 is more poly-reactive than PGZL1, binding to cultured cells and numerous isolated phospholipids even in the absence of antigen.
source: 4E10 is notably more poly-reactive: binding to cultured cells, numerous isolated phospholipids (Matyas et al., 2009), and vesicles of most compositions even in the absence of antigen – whereas 10E8, LN01, and PGZL1 do not.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from cited studies.

claim: PGZL1 and 4E10 crystal structures both bear putative lipid electron density at several surface loops, notably recurring within a CDR-H1 site.
source: PGZL1 and 4E10 crystal structures both bear putative lipid electron density at several surface loops, notably recurring within a CDR-H1 site – a region when mutation reduced the neutralization potency 10-fold for PGZL1-H4K3 (Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2016; Zwick et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallography data from cited studies.

claim: Mutation of the CDR-H1 region reduced neutralization potency 10-fold for PGZL1-H4K3.
source: PGZL1 and 4E10 crystal structures both bear putative lipid electron density at several surface loops, notably recurring within a CDR-H1 site – a region when mutation reduced the neutralization potency 10-fold for PGZL1-H4K3 (Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2016; Zwick et al., 2001).
evidence: This is experimental data from cited studies.

claim: Both 4E10 and PGZL1 showed strong hotspots for a lipid phosphate bound within the CDR-H1 loops in simulations.
source: Upon time-averaging phospholipid density from four independent trajectories, both bnAbs showed strong hotspots for a lipid phosphate bound within the CDR-H1 loops, with minimal phospholipid or cholesterol ordering around the proteins elsewhere.
evidence: This is a finding from the MD simulation data analysis.

claim: The simulated lipid phosphates bound within CDR-H1 have exceptional overlap with electron densities from respective lipid-soaked co-crystal structures of 4E10 and PGZL1, with phosphate mean positions RMSDs of 0.6 and 0.7 Å.
source: The simulated lipid phosphates bound within CDR-H1 have exceptional overlap with electron densities and atomic details of modelled headgroups from respective lipid-soaked co-crystal structures of 4E10 and PGZL1 (Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2017; Irimia et al., 2016), with phosphate mean positions RMSDs of 0.6 and 0.7 Å, respectively, relative to the X-ray structures (Figure 1A, B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between simulation results and experimental structures shown in Figure 1.

claim: The CDR-H1 lipid phosphate complexes are stable, specific interactions that anchor and orient CDR loops at the bilayer surface for antigen engagement.
source: The CDR-H1 lipid phosphate complexes appear to be stable, specific interactions that anchor and orient CDR loops at the bilayer surface for antigen engagement, complementing protein-lipid interactions which are less geometrically specific, that is lipid tail solvation of apolar groups in the CDR-H loops such as CDR-H3 tryptophans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation data regarding the functional role of these complexes.

claim: For both 4E10 and PGZL1, three of four replicates showed very rapid binding of a headgroup phosphate ab initio in the first 20 nanoseconds.
source: For both 4E10 and PGZL1, three of four replicates showed very rapid binding of a headgroup phosphate ab initio in the first 20 nanoseconds (ns) from lipids diffusing in from ≥ 8 Å away (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the simulation trajectories shown in Figure 1C, D.

claim: In some cases, phospholipids bound as early as the protein-restrained equilibration (15 ns) where lipids can freely diffuse.
source: In some cases, phospholipids bound as early as the protein-restrained equilibration (15 ns) where lipids can freely diffuse (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Most phospholipid complexes were highly stable, typically persisting for hundreds of nanoseconds with low mobility of the phosphate headgroup relative to CDR-H1 (<1 Å RMSF) and high overall occupancy (both >80% across 4 µs total).
source: Upon formation, most phospholipid complexes were highly stable, typically persisting for hundreds of nanoseconds with low mobility of the phosphate headgroup relative to CDR-H1 (<1 Å RMSF) and high overall occupancy (both >80% across 4 µs total).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the stability of the phospholipid complexes from simulation data.

claim: An extensive polar network coordinates the lipid phosphate oxygens within the CDR-H1 loop through hydrogen bonds from backbone amides and sidechain hydroxyls.
source: An extensive polar network coordinates the lipid phosphate oxygens within the CDR-H1 loop: hydrogen bonds donated from backbone amides of Phe29 and Ser30 and from sidechain hydroxyls of Ser29/Thr29 and Ser30 (Figure 1C, D; Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the molecular interactions observed in simulations and consistent with cited structures.

claim: CDR-H loops in contact with the membrane maintained internally rigid backbone conformations during simulation with CDR-H1 having <1 Å RMSF.
source: Notably, CDR-H loops in contact with the membrane maintained internally rigid backbone conformations during simulation with CDR-H1 having <1 Å RMSF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of structural stability from the simulation data.

claim: One PGZL1 simulation captured a rare dynamic lipid exchange event where a POPC molecule bound for ~500 ns dissociated and was replaced by a POPA molecule.
source: One PGZL1 simulation captured a rare dynamic lipid exchange event (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; Video 2). A POPC molecule, bound for ~500 ns, dissociated from the CDR-H1 and was promptly replaced by a second nearby lipid, POPA.
evidence: This is a specific observation from one simulation trajectory shown in the supplementary figure and video.

claim: Heavy-chain framework region 3 (FR-H3) extensively intercalates into the bilayer surface for both 4E10 and PGZL1.
source: One novel observation consistent between our 4E10 and PGZL1 simulations was that heavy-chain framework region 3 (FR-H3) extensively intercalates into the bilayer surface.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the simulation data analysis.

claim: Predominantly germline encoded antibody surface features can provide significant contributions to the membrane binding mechanism and surface orientation of antibodies.
source: This finding demonstrates that predominantly germline encoded antibody surface features can provide significant contributions to the membrane binding mechanism and surface orientation of antibodies – a key insight for invoking and honing antibody-lipid interactions in vaccine design.
evidence: This is an interpretation and implication of the FR-H3 finding from simulations.

claim: For the light-chain loops and FR-H3 of PGZL1 and 4E10, charged residues mediate their shallower headgroup surface interactions.
source: For the light-chain loops and FR-H3 of PGZL1 and 4E10, charged residues mediate their shallower headgroup surface interactions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B), whereas the CDR-H loops bare neighboring stretches of hydrophobic and lipophilic polar residues facilitating their deeper embedding.
evidence: This is an analysis of the molecular features mediating membrane interactions from simulation data.

claim: Compared to PGZL1, 4E10's CDR-H loops are further buried, more extensively contacting lipid aliphatic tails, which may explain 4E10's higher tendency for poly-specificity.
source: Compared to PGZL1, 4E10's CDR-H loops are further buried, more extensively contacting lipid aliphatic tails – which may in part explain 4E10's higher tendency for poly-specificity.
evidence: This is an observation from simulation data with a speculative interpretation about poly-specificity.

claim: In all four replicate simulations of 10E8, a POPC complexed at a groove between CDR-L1 and FR-L3.
source: In all four replicate simulations, we observed a POPC complexed at a groove between CDR-L1 and FR-L3 (Figure 2A, B) which had had significant non-protein electron density in previous 10E8 X-ray structures with and without lipids, which had been modelled as headgroup phosphoglycerol anions, glycerol, or free dihydrogen phosphate (Irimia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a consistent finding across all 10E8 simulation replicates.

claim: In 10E8 simulations, the stably bound POPC phosphate was slightly offset (2.7 Å) from the proposed CDR-L1 crystallographic site and instead localized to FR-L3.
source: In our simulations, the stably bound POPC phosphate was slightly offset (2.7 Å) from the proposed CDR-L1 crystallographic site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and instead localized to FR-L3 stabilized by a hydrogen bonding network from Ser83 hydroxyl, Gly84 backbone amide, and Asn85 C-alpha proton (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between simulation results and experimental structures.

claim: In 10E8 simulations, the POPC choline moiety occupied the precise crystallographic CDR-L1 site, coordinated by four pre-organized unpaired backbone carbonyls.
source: Simultaneously, the POPC choline moiety occupied the precise crystallographic CDR-L1 site, wherein the choline cation was coordinated by four pre-organized unpaired backbone carbonyls stemming from the specific CDR-L1 short loop helix conformation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the molecular interactions observed in simulations at the CDR-L1 site.

claim: The bivalent 10E8 phosphocholine complexes at the CDR-L1 FR-L3 groove had >70% occupancy overall across replicate simulations with high stability.
source: We find these bivalent complexes engaging both moieties of the lipid phosphocholine (PC) zwitterion at this CDR-L1 FR-L3 groove with >70% occupancy overall across replicate simulations with high stability: 0.5 Å RMSF for CDR-L1–choline site and 0.5 Å RMSF for FR-L3–phosphate site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of binding stability from simulation data.

claim: The double mutant of R29 and Y38 to alanine in 10E8 exhibited vastly decreased neutralization (>500-fold) across HIV strains with negligible impact to MPER affinity.
source: Previous experiments highlight the importance of CDR-L1 phospholipid binding site features in 10E8's neutralization mechanism, given that the double mutant of R29 and Y38 to alanine exhibited vastly decreased neutralization (>500-fold) across HIV strains with negligible impact to MPER affinity (Irimia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study.

claim: Stable and specific phospholipid binding sites rapidly formed within the respective CDR loop sites for 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8 in membranes with HIV-like cholesterol-rich composition.
source: Thus, these bnAb phospholipid binding sites can accommodate a broader scope of lipid tail and headgroup chemistries possibly beyond those we have investigated here, and can readily form stable phospholipid anchoring complexes in bilayers of HIV-like cholesterol-rich composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion from simulations with more complex membrane compositions.

claim: The CDR-H1 loop backbone conformation of 4E10 and PGZL1 is relatively prevalent in the protein universe, with between 105 to 2∙10^6 geometrically similar sub-segments found in natural proteins.
source: Structural searches querying the lipid-binding loop backbone conformation of each Fab (as previously described Cardoso et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2019; Irimia et al., 2017) identified between 105 to 2∙106 geometrically similar sub-segments within natural proteins (<2 Å RMSD) (Polizzi and DeGrado, 2020), reflecting they are relatively prevalent (not rare) in the protein universe, comparing well with frequency of other surface loops of similar length in antibodies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from structural bioinformatics analysis.

claim: When searching for loops similar to the CDR-H1 of 4E10 and PGZL1, only four cases of phosphate-type ligand binding motifs were identified, making this a realistic but rare protein-phospho-ligand structural motif.
source: When searching for loops similar to the CDR-H1 of 4E10 and PGZL1, only four cases of phosphate-type ligand binding motifs were identified. Thus, this CDR-H1 site is a realistic but rare protein-phospho-ligand structural motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is a result from structural bioinformatics analysis.

claim: For 10E8's CDR-L1 site, only 1 phosphate-type ligand was observed in the structural database search.
source: For 10E8's CDR-L1 site, only 1 phosphate-type ligand was observed: a solvent-exposed surface crystallographic ion.
evidence: This is a result from structural bioinformatics analysis.

claim: 10E8's FR-L3 beta-turn site was a hot spot for phosphate-type ligands, with 23 natural protein cases found.
source: By contrast, 10E8's FR-L3 beta-turn site was a hot spot for phosphate-type ligands, with 23 natural protein cases (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is a result from structural bioinformatics analysis.

claim: Simulated antigen-free Fabs favor similar orientations on lipid bilayer surfaces as in bnAb-bound tilted Env experimental structures.
source: Simulated antigen-free Fabs favor similar orientations on lipid bilayer surfaces as in bnAb-bound tilted Env experimental structures, likely facilitated by the anchoring phospholipid complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and experimental cryo-EM structures.

claim: The primary difference between simulated and cryo-EM Fab orientations is that Env-bound Fabs adopt slightly more shallow approach angles (~15°) relative to the bilayer normal.
source: The primary difference is Env-bound Fabs in cryo-EM adopt slightly more shallow approach angles (~15°) relative to the bilayer normal. The simulated bnAbs in isolation prefer slightly more upright orientations, but present CDRs at approximately the same depth and orientation.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between simulation and experimental data.

claim: Upon clustering the 4E10 ensemble, all substates maintained 86–98% occupancy of the CDR-H1 phospholipid complex.
source: Upon clustering the 4E10 ensemble, interestingly, all substates maintained 86–98% occupancy of the CDR-H1 phospholipid complex, whereas 10E8 and PGZL1 ensemble substates showed more conformation-specific variance in their respective phospholipid binding (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E, G, I).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of phospholipid binding across different conformational states.

claim: Two 10E8 substates exhibit low CDR-L1 PC headgroup occupancy (23%, 33%) due to a domain rotation (20–30°).
source: For example, two 10E8 substates exhibit low CDR-L1 PC headgroup occupancy (23%, 33%) due to a domain rotation (20–30°) resulting in more CDR-H contacts at the expense of the more typical CDR-L interactions typically observed for 10E8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4I).
evidence: This is an analysis of conformational substates and their effect on lipid binding.

claim: LN01 crystal structures bind one phospholipid and one dodecyl-PC detergent in its CDRs.
source: MPER-bound LN01 structures bind one phospholipid and one dodecyl-PC detergent in its CDRs, implying possible paratope-epitope-membrane cooperativity in the neutralization mechanism and two putative phospholipid sites anchoring the bnAb to membrane surfaces (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallography data.

claim: In LN01, the PC headgroup binding site resides in the CDR-H3-L1-L2 inter-chain groove, with the lipid phosphate engaged by CDR-L1 Lys31 via salt bridge and the choline moiety interacting in a cation-pi cage with Tyr32 and CDR-H3 Tyr100g.
source: The PC headgroup binding site resides in the CDR-H3-L1-L2 inter-chain groove, with the lipid phosphate engaged by CDR-L1 Lys31 via salt bridge and the choline moiety interacting in a cation-pi cage with Tyr32 and CDR-H3 Tyr100g. When present, MPER contributes additional choline-aromatic stacking (Trp680, Tyr681).
evidence: This describes the molecular interactions at the LN01 phospholipid binding site from structural data.

claim: The second LN01 phospholipid binding site lies between CDR-H1 and -H2, ordering PS or PC headgroups in crystal structures.
source: The second more solvent-exposed site lies between CDR-H1 and -H2, ordering PS or PC headgroups in crystal structures.
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallography data.

claim: The MPER-antibody interface including key interactions remained stable in LN01 simulations.
source: The MPER-antibody interface including key interactions (e.g. Trp100H to Thr676 H-bond) remained stable.
evidence: This is an observation from the LN01 simulation trajectories.

claim: In both apo and MPER-TM-bound LN01 replicates, several POPC binding events were observed within the CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove at atomic accuracy when compared to dodecyl-PC headgroup position in LN01 X-ray structures.
source: In both apo and MPER-TM-bound replicates, several POPC binding events were observed within the CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove at atomic accuracy when compared to dodecyl-PC headgroup position in LN01 X-ray structures, with the same sidechain interactions (Figure 3E–J).
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and experimental structures.

claim: Phospholipids in LN01's CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove site have much lower kinetic stability and occupancy (~30% and ~40% for MPER-TM-bound and apo, respectively) compared to other bnAbs.
source: In contrast to PGZL1, 4E10, and 10E8 simulations, phospholipids in LN01's CDR-H3-L1-L2 groove site have much lower kinetic stability and occupancy: ~30% and~40% aggregate occupancy for MPER-TM-bound and apo, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of binding occupancy across different antibodies.

claim: An additional new CDR-phospholipid binding site termed the Loading Site was observed reproducibly across apo and MPER-TM-bound LN01 trajectories at a groove comprised of CDR-H2, CDR-H3, and FR-L2.
source: Two interesting behaviors stood out in LN01 simulations. First, an additional new CDR-phospholipid binding site was observed reproducibly across apo and MPER-TM-bound trajectories at an alternative groove comprised of and CDR-H2, CDR-H3, and FR-L2 we termed the Loading Site (Figure 3E–J).
evidence: This is a novel finding from the LN01 simulations.

claim: The Loading site in LN01 was occupied more often than the X-ray site: 78% and 58% simulation time for MPER-TM-bound and apo LN01 replicates respectively.
source: The Loading site was occupied more often than the X-ray site: 78% and 58% simulation time for MPER-TM-bound and apo LN01 replicates respectively (Figure 3I, J; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of binding occupancy from simulation data.

claim: Antigen-free LN01 sampled a broader range of geometries at the membrane surface compared to MPER-TM-bound LN01.
source: The second notable behavior observed was that antigen-free LN01 sampled a broader range of geometries at the membrane surface, characterized by two angles describing the Fab relative to the membrane (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing apo and antigen-bound simulation ensembles.

claim: LN01 complexed with MPER-TM was more deeply and extensively embedded than LN01 alone and resulted in a more focused conformation landscape.
source: LN01 complexed with MPER-TM was more deeply and extensively embedded than LN01 alone and resulted in a more focused conformation landscape – aligned with the minimal dynamics of the MPER-TM orientation.
evidence: This is a comparison of conformational ensembles between apo and antigen-bound states.

claim: Apo LN01 heavily samples the major conformation adopted in MPER-TM-bound state, suggesting LN01's surface-bound geometry is predisposed for transmembrane antigen engagement.
source: Critically, while apo LN01 favors a different geometry (positive Rotation angle) its membrane surface ensemble heavily samples the major conformation adopted in MPER-TM-bound state (negative Rotation angle; Figure 3B, D). This observation that LN01's surface-bound geometry is predisposed for transmembrane antigen engagement suggests that maturing bnAbs' sequences and structures are primed for the membrane interaction key to access MPER and form the neuralization complex.
evidence: This is an observation from simulation data with an interpretation about antibody maturation.

claim: Fab's simulated in CG representation with elastic network restraints maintained the protein fold (<2 Å backbone RMSD) and retained key heavy-light inter-domain contacts.
source: Fab's simulated in CG representation with elastic network restraints maintained the protein fold (<2 Å backbone RMSD) and retained key heavy-light inter-domain contacts, informing that this polar bead model rigidly presents the Fab macroscopic surface features critical for mediating bilayer surface interactions, that is hydrophobic patches, charge, polarity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This validates the CG model by showing it maintains structural integrity.

claim: In 18 replicate spontaneous insertion CG simulations for each of 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, CDR-directed association stable within the lipid bilayer (>1 µs) was observed within 10, 14, and 12 trajectories, respectively.
source: In 18 replicate simulations for each of 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, we observed CDR-directed association stable within the lipid bilayer (>1 µs) within 10, 14, and 12 trajectories, respectively (Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1, Video 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of CG simulation results.

claim: Bovine serum albumin (BSA) showed drastically reduced membrane contact events (2/18) and lack of sustained insertion in CG simulations.
source: As a reference, bovine serum albumin (BSA) was tested similarly. BSA's documented weak affinity for lipid bilayer association (low millimolar; Ruggeri et al., 2013) aligns with the drastically reduced membrane contact events (2/18) and lack of sustained insertion observed (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a negative control result from CG simulations.

claim: Non-neutralizing anti-gp41 antibody 13h11 exhibited negligible insertion and only sparse 'scanning' events in CG simulations.
source: Non-neutralizing anti-gp41 antibody 13h11 having no detectable lipid bilayer interaction by bilayer interferometry (Alam et al., 2009; Nicely et al., 2010) also exhibited negligible insertion and only sparse 'scanning' events, starkly contrasting the bnAbs' behaviors.
evidence: This is a negative control result from CG simulations consistent with experimental data.

claim: CG simulations readily distinguish MPER bnAbs with high propensity for lipid interaction (low micromolar affinity) from non-specific and low affinity lipid interactions.
source: Thus, these CG simulations readily distinguish MPER bnAbs with high propensity for lipid interaction (low micromolar affinity) from non-specific and low affinity lipid interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing bnAb CG simulations with BSA and 13h11 controls.

claim: Fab conformational ensembles and protein-lipid interaction patterns from both CG approaches heavily overlapped with the primary geometry observed for each respective bnAb all-atom trajectories.
source: Fab conformational ensembles and protein-lipid interaction patterns from both CG approaches heavily overlapped with the primary geometry observed for each respective bnAb all-atom trajectories, showing consistency between the two simulation models (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a comparison showing consistency between CG and all-atom simulation results.

claim: CG 4E10 insertions across both methods adopted single conformations which were similar and all-atom-like.
source: CG 4E10 insertions across both methods adopted single conformations which were similar and all-atom-like.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing CG and all-atom simulation results for 4E10.

claim: PGZL1 and 10E8 showed more promiscuity by sampling alternative ab initio membrane-inserted geometries alongside their respective all-atom-like conformations in CG simulations.
source: PGZL1 and 10E8 showed more promiscuity by sampling alternative ab initio membrane-inserted geometries alongside their respective all-atom-like conformations, with these states appearing consistently in both CG approaches but at different frequencies.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing CG simulation results for PGZL1 and 10E8.

claim: For each bnAb, all sustained CG insertion events are CDR-directed.
source: Overall, these CG simulations facilitate study of ab initio membrane insertion for MPER bnAbs, wherein we find all sustained events are CDR-directed, ruling out contributions from other Fab surface features.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from analyzing all CG simulation trajectories.

claim: For each of 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8, three representative medoid Fab poses were extracted by clustering CG simulation frames and converted to all-atom detail to initiate unbiased MD simulation.
source: For each of 4E10, PGZl1, and 10E8, three representative medoid Fab poses were extracted by clustering CG simulation frames (clusters A, B, C), and converting to all-atom detail to initiate unbiased MD simulation (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This describes the methodology for integrating CG and all-atom simulations.

claim: For 4E10, trajectories initiated from all three CG-derived geometries drifted back to conformations very similar to those of initial pre-inserted all-atom trajectories and bound phospholipids at the CDR-H1 site.
source: For 4E10, trajectories initiated from all three geometries drifted back to conformations very similar to those of our initial pre-inserted all-atom trajectories and bound phospholipids at the CDR-H1 site (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This shows that CG-derived conformations converge to biologically relevant states in all-atom simulations.

claim: The 4E10 trajectory back-mapped from CG cluster A adopted deeper insertion and higher CDR-H1 phospholipid binding occupancy (>60%) compared to clusters B and C.
source: Interestingly, the trajectory back-mapped from cluster A adopted deeper insertion and higher CDR-H1 phospholipid binding occupancy (>60%) compared to ensembles of clusters B and C trajectories, which were slightly tilted (rotation angle >0°) and less extensively inserted, indicating the latter geometries are likely less ideal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of different starting conformations and their outcomes.

claim: For PGZL1, all-atom trajectories starting from CG clusters B and C converge to CDR-H-inserted conformations analogous to previous all-atom MD, and stably bind phospholipid headgroups at CDR-H1 (>50% occupancy).
source: For PGZL1, all-atom trajectories starting from CG clusters B and C similarly converge to CDR-H-inserted conformations analogous to our previous all-atom MD, and stably bind phospholipid headgroups at CDR-H1 (>50% occupancy; Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This shows successful integration of CG and all-atom simulations for PGZL1.

claim: For 10E8, the all-atom trajectory from CG Cluster C started and finished in membrane-bound orientations analogous to the pre-inserted simulations and the bivalent CDR-L1 phospholipid complex readily formed with high occupancy (>70%).
source: For 10E8, Cluster C started and finished in membrane-bound orientations analogous to the pre-inserted simulations (Figure 6C), although the Fab adopted a slightly different protein-lipid interaction pattern with much shallower CDR-H3 insertion, the bivalent CDR-L1 phospholipid complex still readily formed with high occupancy (>70%) (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This shows successful integration of CG and all-atom simulations for 10E8.

claim: The all-atom simulation from one alternate 10E8 CG conformation (cluster A) rapidly dissociated from the membrane within 50 ns, showing this integrative MD distinguishes this state as an unstable likely artifact.
source: All-atom simulation from one alternate conformation of 10E8, CG cluster A, rapidly dissociated from the membrane within 50 ns (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), showing this integrative MD distinguishes this state as an unstable likely artifact.
evidence: This demonstrates that the integrative approach can identify unstable/artifactual conformations.

claim: With one membrane-bound Fab, it is very unlikely a second Fab can simultaneously engage the bilayer due to restriction from the IgG hinge.
source: The resulting full-length IgG geometries shows that with one membrane-bound Fab, it is very unlikely a second Fabs can simultaneously engage the bilayer due to restriction from the IgG hinge – except for the case of an extraordinarily flexible hinge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is an inference from modeling full-length IgG based on Fab orientations.

claim: Biased constant velocity atomistic simulations were applied to compute the force required to dissociate a Fab bound to lipid bilayers, providing a binding strength estimate akin to force spectroscopy.
source: Finally, we applied biased constant velocity atomistic simulations to compute the force required to dissociate a Fab bound to lipid bilayers – providing a binding strength estimate akin to force spectroscopy (Figure 7A).
evidence: This describes the methodology for estimating membrane binding strength.

claim: 4E10 WAWA variant has similar Kd to MPER as 4E10, but significantly reduced affinity to empty HIV-like liposomes and neutralization efficacy (>100-fold higher IC50).
source: WAWA has similar Kd to MPER as 4E10, but significantly reduced affinity to empty HIV-like liposomes and neutralization efficacy (>100-fold higher IC50; Scherer et al., 2010; Kwon et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2010; Montero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is experimental data from cited studies.

claim: Across replicates from different starting states for 4E10 (n=9) and WAWA (n=11), rupture force calculations showed average forces of 63.8±2.8 kJ/nm/mol and 48.0±2.6 kJ/nm/mol, respectively.
source: Across replicates from different starting states for 4E10 (n=9) and WAWA (n=11), rupture force calculations showed average forces (± S.E.M.) of 63.8±2.8 kJ/nm/mol and 48.0±2.6 kJ/nm/mol, respectively (Figure 7D, E), correctly indicating the 4E10 ensemble has a stronger membrane interaction (32 ± 13%; p-value <0.001).
evidence: This is quantitative data from pulling simulations showing statistically significant differences.

claim: Mature PGZL1 has relatively high affinity to the MPER epitope peptide (Kd = 10 nM) and demonstrates great breadth and potency, neutralizing 84% of a 130-strain panel.
source: Mature PGZL1 has relatively high affinity to the MPER epitope peptide (Kd = 10 nM) and demonstrates great breadth and potency, neutralizing 84% of a 130-strain panel.
evidence: This is experimental data characterizing mature PGZL1.

claim: An 'Intermediate' PGZL1 with V-gene germline reversion (gVmDmJ) showed a modest affinity loss (Kd = 64 nM), while neutralization potency and breadth (12%) were more substantially reduced than expected due to affinity alone.
source: An 'Intermediate' PGZL1 with V-gene germline reversion (gVmDmJ, 100% CDR-H3 identity) showed a modest affinity loss (Kd = 64 nM), while neutralization potency and breadth (12%) were more substantially reduced than expected due to affinity alone – attributed to impaired lipid bilayer interactions (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is experimental data from a cited study.

claim: The fully 'Germline' reverted PGZL1 variant (gVgDgM) had no detectable MPER peptide affinity or neutralization.
source: The fully 'Germline' reverted variant (gVgDgM) had no detectable MPER peptide affinity or neutralization.
evidence: This is experimental data characterizing germline PGZL1.

claim: Significantly lower pulling forces were required to dissociate Intermediate and Germline PGZL1 from bilayers (37.5±14.9 and 41.2±11.7 kJ/nm/mol respectively) than for mature PGZL1 (56.1±11.6 kJ/nm/mol; p<0.003).
source: Significantly lower pulling forces were required to dissociate Intermediate and Germline PGZL1 from bilayers, 37.5±14.9 kJ/nm/mol and 41.2±11.7 kJ/nm/mol respectively, than for mature PGZL1, 56.1±11.6 kJ/nm/mol (p<0.003; Figure 7E).
evidence: This is quantitative data from pulling simulations showing statistically significant differences.

claim: The difference in Germline and Intermediate PGZL1 force distributions was not significant (p>0.4).
source: While the difference in Germline and Intermediate force distributions was not significant (p>0.4), more higher force events were observed for the Intermediate.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the pulling simulation data.

claim: bnAb phospholipid binding features are acquired and honed along the maturation pathway, connecting positive selection of antibody-lipid interactions with neutralization efficacy.
source: These results provide further evidence that bnAb phospholipid binding features are acquired and honed along the maturation pathway, entrenching the connection between positive selection of antibody-lipid interactions and neutralization efficacy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the PGZL1 variant pulling simulation results.

claim: Initial membrane-bound Fab conformations were computed using PPM2.0, globally optimizing protein insertion based on per-residue hydrophobicity and solvation.
source: Initial membrane-bound Fab conformations were computed using PPM2.03735 (Lomize et al., 2012), globally optimizing protein insertion based on per-residue hydrophobicity and solvation, each resulting in reasonable predictions with CDR-H3 embedded.
evidence: This describes the computational method used to generate initial structures.

claim: The coordinates for Fab models were obtained from X-ray crystallography structures (PDB id: 2FX9, 6O3D, 5T85 for 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8 respectively).
source: The coordinates for Fab models were obtained from X-ray crystallography structures for each antibody (PDB id: 2FX9, 6O3D, 5T85 for 4E10, PGZL1, and 10E8 respectively).
evidence: This describes the source of structural models used in the study.

claim: Atomistic simulations were performed with Gromacs 2021 and CHARMM36 forcefield.
source: Atomistic simulations were performed with Gromacs 2021 and CHARMM36 forcefield.
evidence: This describes the simulation software and parameters used.

claim: A 2 fs time step was used along with the LINCS constraint algorithm during the equilibration stage of atomistic simulations.
source: A 2 fs time step was used along with the LINCS constraint algorithm during the equilibration stage.
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters used.

claim: Coarse grain representations of Fab models were generated based on the Martini version 2.2 four to one mapping of heavy atoms to bead representation.
source: Coarse grain representations of Fab models were generated based on the Martini version 2.2 four to one mapping of heavy atoms to bead representation using the martinize script with an elastic network that defined harmonic bonds at default parameters.
evidence: This describes the coarse-graining methodology used.
